sections.authorBiography: Washington Irving was born in New York City on 3 April 1783, the youngest of eleven children of a merchant family, and named after George Washington. He won fame with a comic History of New York (1809) by "Diedrich Knickerbocker" and lived in England from 1815, where he published The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. (1819–20), containing "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow." He was among the first American writers admired in Europe; he later served as U.S. minister to Spain and died at Sunnyside, his home in Tarrytown, New York, on 28 November 1859.
sections.historicalContext: Set around 1790 in a Dutch settlement near Tarrytown, New York, a region full of Revolutionary War ghost stories. The Headless Horseman is said to be a Hessian soldier (a German mercenary fighting for Britain) whose head was shot off by a cannonball.

publicationAndReception.publication: Published in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. (part VI, 1820).
publicationAndReception.now: One of the first American ghost stories; a Halloween classic, often adapted.

sections.overview: Ichabod Crane, a lanky, superstitious schoolmaster from Connecticut, courts the wealthy Katrina Van Tassel, competing with the local hero Brom Bones.
sections.whyItMatters: It's a model of humour, suspense and ambiguous endings.

spoilerOverview.text: Riding home from a party, Ichabod is chased by the Headless Horseman, who hurls his head; Ichabod disappears, a smashed pumpkin is found, and Brom marries Katrina, looking knowing whenever the pumpkin is mentioned.

lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 6–10 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Legend of Sleepy Hollow: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

shortAnswer: Explain how superstition and imagination develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how greed and courtship develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how rural community develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (superstition and imagination, greed and courtship, rural community) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Legend of Sleepy Hollow teaches about superstition and imagination. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Washington Irving develops superstition and imagination in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Washington Irving develops superstition and imagination across The Legend of Sleepy Hollow. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of superstition and imagination. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of superstition and imagination in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Washington Irving's choices in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of superstition and imagination, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Legend of Sleepy Hollow's treatment of superstition and imagination in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on superstition and imagination in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on superstition and imagination in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about superstition and imagination in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on superstition and imagination in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
